title: Roaming Charges: History Hurts
author: Jeffrey St. Clair
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/explodingtrees-680x453.avif)

Crosswhite Fire, Central Oregon. Photo: Bryan Longoria, Oregon Department of
Forestry, Incident Management Team 3.

> “History is what hurts.”
>
> – Frederic Jameson

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/langsodyssey-680x383.png)

The Gods manipulating events in Fritz Lang's "Odysseus", the film within a
film, in Godard's Le Mépris.

It was 92 in the shade and we fled to the nearest theater to escape the heat
and the shrouds of smoke from distant fires that had drifted across the
Cascades into the Valley. The movie was “The Odyssey.” Christopher Nolan’s The
Odyssey, not Homer’s, which quickly became apparent. The screen was 28 meters
wide, roughly the width, by the way, of the theater of Dionysus on the south
slope of the Acropolis in Athens, where many plays depicting episodes from the
Trojan War and the homecoming were performed. The cost of the ticket was $35,
much cheaper than the [$1,000](https://www.fox5ny.com/news/odyssey-tickets-
imax-70-mm-nyc-selling-over-1000) some New Yorkers have shelled out for the
chance to watch the three-hour epic on 70mm IMAX screens, through the latest
innovation of late-capitalism, dynamic pricing. (Thank you, Bruce
Springsteen.) In 4th-century Athens, the city-state comped entry fees for the
25,000 people who would assemble to watch the plays of Aeschylus, Sophocles
and Euripides. Maybe Mamdani will provide a city subsidy for at least a bag of
popcorn, which now costs more than a movie ticket did a decade ago, when there
was still a film industry in the US.

The less said about Nolan’s film, the better. Frankly, there’s not much to
critique. It is what it is, a spectacle in search of a reason to exist, like
Cleopatra or Ben Hur or Gone With the Wind. It’s not history. It’s not
literature. It’s an entertainment. It’s, in the words of a pretty astute
cultural critic: “a joke.” 173 minutes summed up in two words. Top that,
Pauline Kael. It is a joke, but alas, not a funny one. Christopher Nolan has
no sense of humor. Neither did his hero Stanley Kubrick, but Kubrick at least
had the smarts to hire screenwriters like Terry Southern, who did, and actors
like Peter Sellers, who could inject a jolt of life into an otherwise dreary
exercise in literature-to-big-screen hokum like _Lolita._

The funniest thing Nolan did was to cast Matt Damon as Odysseus, the great
prankster of Greek literature and not give him one funny line, not even a pun.
Nolan has populated his films with recognizable faces, an all-star lineup of
Hollywood celebrities. Some of them are fine actors. But not in this film.
None of the actors act. They pose and speak, stilted words, arthritic phrases.
(In a revealing casting choice, Menelaus, Helen’s cuckolded and abusive
husband who scars her face to despoil her legendary beauty, was played by
[John
Bernthal](https://www.reddit.com/r/popculturechat/comments/1mc0coc/why_does_no_one_ever_talk_about_how_jon_bernthal/),
an outspoken defender of Israel’s genocidal rampages in Gaza, who invited ex-
Israeli special forces soldiers onto his Call to Arms and praised their "wet-
work".)

Nolan doesn’t need actors. There’s little room for acting here. Nolan said
that because he insists on shooting with 70 mm IMAX cameras, he can only film
for three minutes at a time.  The demands of character development and
emotional depth must be sacrificed to the demands of action. How can Odysseus
have the time to think about what he has done or what he will do, when a jump
cut must be made every couple of minutes to a new scene of peril? In fact,
Nolan doesn't even need much of a script. It's all about the images, even when
the montage of images is inchoate. The classics scholar [Emily
Wilson](https://www.wyomingnews.com/news/entertainment/odyssey-translator-
emily-wilson-rips-apart-film-says-shed-be-ashamed-to-have-written-
script/article_9d2394e7-1077-4928-bd68-265173cb2ef2.html), whose vivid and
energetic new translation of _The Odyssey_ Nolan claimed to have consulted for
his film, scorched the film, saying she would have been “ashamed to have
written any part” of the screenplay.

The heresy, if that’s what you want to call it, in casting Zendaya as Athena
and Lupita Nyong'o as Helen (and her sister Clytemnestra) isn’t that they are
black actors but that the allegedly “woke” Christopher Nolan gave these black
actors so little to do. Like Helen, Nyont’o is one of the world’s most
beautiful humans, a rarefied model of the perfection of the species. And that
captivating allure shines through her scar-riven face. Nolan gives her a
handful of lines, merely to advance the plot. But how does Helen feel about
being dragged back to Sparta, bound as a sex-slave and war trophy to the dull-
witted man who shredded her face and killed her lover? We’re left in the dark.

Athena may well have been black (see: Martin Bernal’s _Black Athena: The
Afroasiatic Roots of Classical Civilization_). As one of the supreme Olympian
deities, she was certainly capable of assuming whatever form or skin color she
desired and Zendaya may well be the closest living human to a goddess on
Earth. But Nolan has her do little more than console Odysseus, while wrapped
in a drab woven cloak, looking like Mary Magdalene, patting Jesus on the back.
But this is Athena, the great intellect and warrior goddess, who, consumed by
petty jealousy (See: the Judgement of Paris), plotted and enabled the sacking
of Troy and the genocide of the Trojans and provided a shield of LAPD-like
impunity for her favorite killer. We’d like to hear her explain herself.

I’m a little dismayed at MAGA’s hostility toward Nolan. After all, he shares
their rosy nostalgia for a past that never existed. He wants to Make Cinema
Grand Again in the tradition of Griffith, DeMille, and Ford. Big pictures with
big budgets made only on film (despite its environmental consequences)
projected onto big screens in big movie palaces. Big, big, big. All of it
backed by bankers, private equity, insurers and reinsurers. Nolan's
megalomania is almost Trumpian. But surely the future of movie-making, if it
has a future, is elsewhere. At the end of his life, Jean-Luc Godard was making
movies shot on his iPhone and found it liberating. The two breakout films of
the summer, Obsession and Backrooms, were made by former YouTubers. Why go
back? Why chain yourself to the demands of the money men and cinema owners?

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/zc2S4XgAnCo7mUSRrNYoFE-680x510.jpg)

The procession of Odysseus's Horse into Troy. Giovanni Domenico Tiepolo, 1760.
National Gallery, London.

A genocide has taken place. A city has been burnt to the ground by an invading
force. All of its men have been killed, even the boys. Its women have been
raped. Some of them have been taken back in cages as property of the killers.
A man is adrift on a makeshift raft in the Mediterranean, fleeing the war
zone, a refuge of sorts, looking for a homeland. Who is this man? Where is he
going? What does he want?

He’s a killer. He’s a conman. He is a liar, a thief, a plunderer. He’s a
rapist, an adulterer, a child killer, and a blasphemer. He’s committed
genocide. He’s a head case. He’s haunted by the past. Wracked by the things
he’s done and the travails he’s endured trying to get home, if home is really
where he wants to get. He’s the earliest case of PTSD in literature. He’s
Odysseus!

These are the elements of a story that speaks across the ages to our own
moment of genocide, plunder, tyranny, exile and refugees. But Nolan’s film
doesn’t. In fact, it’s hard to say what Nolan’s film does and why he wanted to
make a film called The Odyssey and not, say, another space opera. He gets so
much wrong about the poem that you wonder why he was attracted to the story in
the first place. It’s the ultimate act of hubris to rewrite Homer, which is
fine, if you've got the chops. James Joyce did it, but Nolan is not Joyce,
even in his own limited medium of film. He’s not even the Cohen Brothers.

Nolan says he was only able to make the Odyssey because of the huge box office
returns from his previous film, Oppenheimer. And in a sense, the Odyssey is
the perfect sequel to Oppenheimer.

The Odyssey is a sequel, in many ways, to Nolan’s previous film, Oppenheimer,
a heroic treatment of the man who designed the atom bomb. Here is the story of
genocider, turned into a hero, because of his ceaseless determination to find
his way home. But how ceaseless was Odysseus's desire for home, really?

What happens after the bomb goes off? What happens after the mass killing?
Odysseus gets lost. He gets lost in his own mind. Is he consumed by guilt or
his own hubris? Hubris was a big thing for the Greeks. All their heroes seemed
to have it and nearly all were undone by it. It was hubris that led Odysseus
to set an uncharted course home to Ithaka. It was hubris that prompted him to
shoot a parting arrow at Polyphemus, enraging his father Poseidon. It was
hubris that sent him to the land of the Lotus Eaters. It was hubris that made
him raid the Cicones, destroy their city, commit genocidal slaughter again,
steal and rape the women. It was hubris that made him open the bag of winds.
Hubris that made him try to loot the land of the Laestrygonians (who appear
briefly in Nolan's film in shiny armor like giant versions of the Arthurian
knights in Bresson's _Lancelot du Lac_), with fatal consequences for his crew.
And on and on.

In his much too brief life, Rainer Werner Fassbinder made 44 films, including
some of the best in the history of cinema. The combined cost of all those
films was less than the cost of Christopher Nolan's $250 million production of
The Odyssey. In fact, you could add the cost of all 40 of Jean Renoir's films
to Fassbinder's and still have enough left over for Agnès Varda to have made a
film or two. Varda could have made a film of the Odyssey for a few dollars,
relatively speaking, which would have mined the misogyny of the Greek heroes,
including the main man, and celebrated the retribution of the women they’ve
abused and betrayed. Because Nolan portrays Odysseus as a hero, longing to
return home to his wife, the faithful Penelope, he elides Odysseus’s great
sin, an act as dark and depraved as anything an ISIS fighter or US GI at My
Lai did. He’s slaughtered the innocent. He’s tricked them into sacrificial
deaths.

In Hades, Agamemnon rises from the grave to tell Odysseus the story of his own
homecoming, bearing Cassandra, the soothsaying princess of Troy, back with him
to Mycenae in a cage as booty, only to be slaughtered in his own bed by his
wife, Clytemnestra. The maniacal king warns Odysseus that he might face a
similar fate in Ithaka. Odysseus has reason for concern, for reasons Nolan
doesn’t explore. His wife Penelope is Clytemnestra’s cousin and she’s likely
to have learned of his own role in the vile killing of Clytemnestra’s
daughter, Iphigenia. As the Greek fleet assembled in the port town of Aulis,
Agamemnon decided to go hunting in Artemis’s sacred grove, where he killed a
deer, enraging the goddess, who loved animals more than men. Artemis calmed
the winds and Agamemnon’s invasion force was stuck in port until, warns the
priest Calchas, the king sacrifices his own child. Odysseus comes up with the
plan. He persuades Clytemnestra and Iphigenia that the young girl will be wed
to the great warrior Achilles and escorts her back to Aulis and places her on
the sacrificial rock where her father slits her throat. It would be easier to
rehabilitate Harvey Weinstein than Odysseus.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Wall_painting_-
_sacrifice_of_Iphigenia_-_Pompeii_VI_8_5_-_Napoli_MAN_9112_-_01.jpg)

Odysseus and Diomedes hauling Iphegenia to her death at Aulis. Fresco from
Pompeii.

Penelope must know this. She was Clytemnestra’s cousin. She had lived in
Mycenae. She was Iphegenia’s aunt. Odysseus had every reason to delay coming
home to her. After all, Penelope, the siren calling from Ithaka, means a kind
of predatory seabird, a kingfisher, a fisher for kings. And like Iphigenia,
Penelope was once sacrificed by her own parents, who had cast her off the
cliff into the sea, only to see her saved by the very birds for whom she was
named.

What does Penelope think? How does she really feel about the man who left her
and took his time coming home, philandering and killing across the
Mediterranean? We don’t know. Nolan doesn’t tell us. He doesn’t understand
women. They’ve always been one-dimensional characters in his films. But she
wasn’t for the Greeks. There’s an ambiguity to Penelope, a mystique, if you
will, that makes you ask, how much she's really yearning for her lost husband.
After all, she isn't weaving a shroud to honor Odysseus, but his aged father,
Laertes, who stayed home, faithful to her, her son and Ithaka.

Penelope was exalted in early Christian theology for her fidelity. But you
can’t say the same for our hero. While he may have been mesmerized by Calypso,
he spent a year canoodling with Circe of his own volition. He wasn’t all that
eager to get back to Penelope’s bedchamber. But Nolan elides this telling
detail from his film.

Only the brooding nymph Calypso succeeds in slowing Odysseus down. The
wanderer stays seven years on Ogygia. But there’s little time for
contemplation in Nolan’s slaughter fest. The seven years in Calypso’s thrall
are squeezed into seven minutes of film and Calypso is reduced to the role of
Odysseus’ therapist, feeding him lotus flowers like Prozac. Is Calypso a
Freudian or Jungian? We don’t know. We don’t even learn what’s really bugging
him or how he exorcizes his demons enough to apologize to Poseidon, the earth-
shaker, and ride the current back to Ithaka. What did he learn? To honor the
dead, maybe. But he would continue to make many more of them.

But this is not Calypso’s role in the Odyssey. She is another avenging proto-
feminist, who tricks the trickster Odysseus and keeps him captive for seven
years, taking her pleasure with him, doing to Odysseus what Odysseus would
have done to her and had done to the Trojan women.

In _The Odyssey,_ Odysseus doesn’t unload his story to Calypso, but to King
Alcinous of the Phaiacians and his enchanting daughter Nausicca on the island
of Scheria (Corfu), a city-state which treated sea-borne immigrants like
Odysseus with kindness and hospitality, a running theme of Homer’s poem, which
Nolan manages to mangle.

There are unanswered questions, left hanging, because of the box office. What
are the sirens singing, “each to each,” Eliot put it. Are they singing songs
of seduction, tempting him into the fatal waters? Or are they singing songs of
horror, threnodies for the needless death, tempting him to drown himself in
shame? Nolan doesn’t even hint at the answer, for there’s another thrilling
episode just a few scenes away. This is high-T film-making, cinematics for the
manosphere. It’s gotta move, baby. The warrior ethic ain’t got time for
introspection.

We see them only at a distance, women lounging on rocks. For the Greeks, the
sirens had the bodies of birds. They sang songs of death. They were made by
the Goddess Demeter to search the Underworld for her daughter Persephone,
who’d been taken into the eternal darkness by Hades to be his bride. Were they
taunting Odysseus with shades of the men and women he sent there?

The historian Mary Beard ridiculed Nolan’s film for its lack of sex, which, as
Freud made clear, is the driving force behind almost all Greek drama and
comedy. But Nolan doesn’t do Eros. He’s only comfortable in the horrorshow
realm of Thanatos.

The most generous thing that can be said about Nolan's film is that it's a
movie about a man who has committed genocide and who is so mentally unbalanced
by the experience that he kills and plunders all the way home, making one bad
decision after another, until every member of his own army has joined the
ranks of the dead. Then he finally arrives home, where he cleanses his bad
conscience–to the extent he has a conscience–by killing nearly every man left
in Ithaka, especially savoring the murder of a draft-dodging suitor of
Penelope, someone who didn’t want to go slaughter Trojans to open the trade
routes for the tyrannical Agamemnon. This final act of mass violence instructs
his previously non-violent son Telemachus how to kill too, so that he can
become king and the killing can go generation after generation. Nolan tacks on
an ending that’s more Lord of the Rings than the Odyssey, as Penelope and
Nolan’s now sanctified-through-more-blood hero Odysseus set sail for the West
to honor the dead, but only the Greeks, not the Trojans whose entire
population Odysseus and Agamemnon have wiped out.

In Homer’s poem, a truer ending takes place. The mass slaughter at the palace
is greeted with rage by the populace, who gather to storm the gates, until
Athena, once again, intervenes to save her own private mercenary, Odysseus. He
just can’t stop killing. If Homer had enjoyed Cassandra's gift (or curse) of
prophecy, he too might have had Odysseus setting sail into the West to spread
the genocidal method to the nascent empire across the sea.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/godardcontempt-680x387.png)

Still from Jean-Luc Godard's Le Mépris.

The greatest cinematic version of _The Odyssey_ is a film about the absurdity
of making a film about _The Odyssey_ , Godard’s _Le Mépris_ (Contempt), where
Michel Piccoli’s character is hired by an American producer (Jack Palance) to
rewrite the script for a film of the Odyssey being shot on Capri by Fritz
Lang. Piccoli brings his wife with him to Italy, herself a living goddess,
Bridget Bardot, whose ravishing beauty and erotic allure overshadow all of the
characters in Lang’s film. Ultimately, Bardot, unlike Penelope, wastes little
time leaving her husband, who is lost in the endless rewrites of the script,
and runs off with the American moneyman to their own rendezvous with tragedy.

Godard’s movie was made for $1 million, double the amount of any of his
previous films. Half of the budget went to Bardot’s fee. Even so, the images
of the film within a film, shot by arguably the greatest cinematographer in
the history of film, Raoul Coutard, are more evocative and visually entrancing
than scenes in Nolan’s made-for-IMAX production. (IMAXxing is the looksmaxxing
of the film industry.) Le Mépris can almost be seen as a prescient parody of
Nolan's–with better acting, editing and cinematography.

If you're thinking about going to see the Odyssey, I’d recommend renting
Pasolini's Medea and Oedipus Rex instead, films made by a poet who understood
the contemporary resonances of the poetic myths he was reenacting.

Alexander Cockburn's favorite writers. Alex was especially enthused by his

second volume of his own memoirs The Golden Age is In Us, which he attributed

book was published, a letter arrived in Petrolia from Paris, bearing the
return address of Claude Lévi-Strauss, informing that Alex that the phrase
belonged to Rousseau, not him. In what I came to call the Cockburn Pirouette,
Alex used this “l’erreur" to justify his hatred of fact-checkers, telling me
as he waved the letter in front of my face: "Now, Jeffrey, imagine if Verso
had fact-checked the Golden Age. I'd never have received a handwritten note
from the greatest genius of our time."

had sex for the first time, the French resistance fighter Hèléne Rytman (his
future wife and 8 years his senior), Althusser was so traumatized and
depressed by the experience (he said he felt only “repulsion”) that he was
committed to the psych ward at Sainte-Anne Hospital in Paris, where he was
subjected to 24 electroshock sessions. Thirty-two years later, Althusser would
strangle Rytman to death in their suite at the École Supérieure Normale in
what the investigating psychiatrists described as “an iatrogenic hallucinatory
episode complicated by melancholic depression.” Althusser was deemed mentally
incompetent to stand trial and was once again locked up in the psych ward,
from which he would never return. In his memoir, _L’Avenir Dure
Longtemps_(_The Future Lasts Forever_), Althusser claimed he killed her out of
love: I killed a woman who was everything to me during a crisis of mental
confusion, she who loved me to the point of wanting only to die because she
could not continue living. And no doubt in my confusion and unconsciousness I
'did her this service,' which she did not try to prevent, but from which she
died.” But several friends of Rytman say she was on the brink of leaving him
when he squeezed the life out of her, as she lay prone on their bed.
Althusser, the celebrated Marxist, who admitted later in life that he’d only
read volume one of Capital and was MIA during the May ’68 protests while his
aging nemesis Jean-Paul Sartre was on the streets with rebellious students,
spent the rest of his years confined to mental hospitals outside Paris, first
in Soisy-sur-Seine, then the Centre Marcel Rivière in La Verrière. The
vicissitudes of Althusser’s confinement and attempts to “heal” his mental
“disorder” wouldn’t have surprised his former student, Michel Foucault.

\+ When you're scanning the shelves of Portland's most eccentric (and probably
best) used bookstore, Mother Foucault's, don't insult Poseidon or you might
spend the next 10 years wandering the stacks, looking for the exit, which, all
things considered, might be a welcome alternative to what's going down
outside. My haul for the afternoon: a copy of Melville’s Benito Cereno in
print large enough for my eroded eyes to read, a collection of Hemingway’s war
journalism, an illustrated cultural history of Paris’ outer ring, the 13th
through 20th Arrondissements, illustrated with peculiar line drawings and
hand-drawn maps, post-911 “dialogues” with Jurgen Habermas and Jacques Derrida
on “terrorism,” Derrida’s own Dissemenations, a history of Indian art, a large
format book on the photography of Native Americans, the poet William Bronk’s
volume Life Supports, CP contributor Ken Knabb’s 1991 book, The Relevance of
Rexroth–all for less than $100, even in the time of Trumpflation. The problem
is, of course, that I’ve been trying to, as the librarians say, deaccession
the ziggurat-like mounds of books on the floor of my office, in the halls, in
the bedroom, but they keep growing, instead….
